name: Top of the basilar syndrome
presentation: A patient suddenly becomes drowsy or briefly unresponsive and, on waking, has vertical gaze palsy, pupils that are small or unequal and react poorly, sometimes skew deviation, and visual field loss that can amount to cortical blindness. Some report vivid formed hallucinations or confabulate cheerfully. Limb weakness is often surprisingly mild for such a dramatic picture, because the embolus lodged at the basilar bifurcation and spared the pons.

deficits.sign: Somnolence or coma from the paramedian midbrain and thalamic reticular projections
Vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, skew deviation
Small, unequal or poorly reactive pupils from pretectal and third nerve nuclear involvement
Hemianopia or cortical blindness from bilateral PCA infarcts

reasoning: An embolus arriving up the basilar artery stops at its bifurcation, where it obstructs the thalamoperforating and mesencephalic perforators and one or both posterior cerebral arteries. The paramedian midbrain contains the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF and the posterior commissure, which generate and cross the vertical gaze commands, the oculomotor nuclei with their Edinger–Westphal components, and the ascending reticular activating system, so vertical gaze, pupils and arousal are all affected bilaterally. The thalamoperforators supply the medial thalamus, adding amnesia and confusion, and the posterior cerebral arteries carry the crossed visual pathways to both occipital lobes, so bilateral occlusion causes cortical blindness with preserved pupils when the pretectum is spared. The corticospinal tracts pass through the crus and pons below the level of the embolus and cross far below in the medulla, so the classic case has little weakness. When the clot extends back into the basilar trunk the syndrome merges with a basilar occlusion and the outcome becomes far worse.

imagingFindings.finding: Filling defect at the basilar bifurcation with absent flow in one or both P1 segments and the thalamoperforators.
Restricted diffusion in the paramedian midbrain, medial thalami and occipital lobes, frequently bilateral.
Dense basilar artery on non-contrast CT; check when a patient presents with unexplained coma.

mimics.name: Metabolic coma
mimics.howToDistinguish: No vertical gaze palsy or pupillary asymmetry; symmetric brainstem reflexes

mimics.name: Non-convulsive status epilepticus
mimics.howToDistinguish: EEG; fluctuating awareness without the ocular signs

mimics.name: Artery of Percheron infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral medial thalamic infarcts without occipital involvement

management: Look for a cardiac source of embolism
